title: Non-Adversarial Imitation Learning Provably Free of Compounding Errors: The Value Flow Mechanism
claim: Prior Q-based imitation gives uniform, uninformative values off the demonstration; ours propagates value to unvisited states and recovers expert actions.
layout: Legend on top, 3 panels left-to-right: environment, prior, ours; shared grid
description: A top legend box explains the encodings: a blue gradient for the state value V(s), a purple gradient for the action value Q(s,a) drawn as triangles, a yellow-outlined triangle for the greedy action, and red equal signs for all Q-values being equal. Below are three 5x5 gridworld panels. (a) shows the plain task: gray wall cells, a cyan goal in the bottom-right, and a yellow expert path running down the left side and along the bottom. (b) shows IQ-Learn: cells on the demonstration path are dark blue, and unvisited cells are pale with four-way arrows and red equal signs, so no action is preferred. (c) shows Dual Q-DM: the same grid has graded blue shading, and unvisited cells have yellow-outlined greedy triangles pointing toward the expert path. The eye goes to the contrast between the red equal signs in (b) and the yellow arrows in (c).
caption: Illustration of the learned Q-functions on a Gridworld task. (a): The Gridworld environment with wall states (gray), goal state (cyan), and one demonstration trajectory (yellow). (b): IQ-Learn's Q-function: visited states acquire high V-values (dark blue), but unvisited states exhibit equal Q-values across all actions (red equal signs), confirming that IQ-Learn cannot identify expert actions beyond demonstrations ([ref]). (c): Dual Q-DM's Q-function: Bellman constraints enable value flow from demonstrated to unvisited states, yielding a structured Q-function whose greedy action (yellow-outlined triangle) at unvisited states correctly points toward the expert trajectory, demonstrating generalization beyond demonstrations ([ref]).
abstract: Adversarial imitation learning (AIL) achieves high-quality imitation by mitigating compounding errors inherent to behavioral cloning (BC), yet its adversarial optimization frequently leads to training instability. A class of non-adversarial Q-based imitation learning (IL) methods, exemplified by IQ-Learn, has emerged to address this instability and is widely believed to outperform BC by leveraging online environment interactions. In this paper, we revisit IQ-Learn and prove that it in fact reduces to BC: it admits an imitation gap lower bound with quadratic dependence on the horizon and therefore remains susceptible to compounding errors. Our theoretical analysis reveals why online interactions fail to help: IQ-Learn uniformly suppresses Q-values for all actions at states not covered by demonstrations, preventing generalization beyond demonstrations. To address this fundamental limitation, we introduce Dual Q-DM, a new Q-based IL method built on Bellman constraints. Crucially, Bellman constraints drive value flow: Q-values propagate from demonstrated to unvisited states through environment dynamics, enabling generalization beyond demonstrations. We prove that Dual Q-DM is equivalent to AIL and can recover expert actions at unvisited states, thereby mitigating compounding errors. To the best of our knowledge, Dual Q-DM is the first non-adversarial IL method that is theoretically guaranteed to eliminate compounding errors. Experimental results further corroborate our theoretical findings.
